newsitem.title: ZAIRE: FEATURE-Mediterranean merchants weather change in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mediterranean merchants weather change in Zaire.

text.p: Political change in Africa can be trying, even for those hardy merchant adventurers who left their homes in the east Mediterranean to make their fortunes as shopkeepers in the heart of the continent.
Christos Hagigeorgiou, a Cypriot from the pretty and prosperous town of Paphos, should know. In 43 years in Zaire, he's upped stakes twice in response to political crises.
But this time, when Laurent Kabila's rebel forces swept through the southeastern mining city of Lubumbashi en route to final victory in Kinshasa, it was a different story.

"We did close up shop for one afternoon but there wasn't any looting. What's really good news is that the dollar has gone down. That means our wage bill is lower and people have more money to spend," he told Reuters in the backroom of his thriving wholesale-retail business in Lubumbashi market.
Like the 200 Lebanese and 300 Greeks who call Lubumbashi home, Hagigeorgiou has learnt to go with the flow, keeping his eyes firmly fixed on the balance sheet and away from politics.
"We always follow the authorities and accept everything they say. We pay all our taxes and customs," he said.
SOME PUT IN JAIL UNTIL THEY PAID THEIR TAXES

Some Lebanese in the central city of Mbuji-Mayi, the heart of the diamond mining industry and a magnet for smugglers, did run into trouble with the new authorities, but those in Lubumbashi have little sympathy for that bunch.

"They produced bits of paper signed by generals and the sons of people close to president Mobutu (Sese Seko). Some of them spent a while in jail until they paid their taxes, then they left the country," said one Lebanese merchant.
Mobutu has fled into exile, yielding power to Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces, a movement which is trying to enforce higher standards in public life.
"Bribes? That's something we were pretty well used to in the old days. Now it's all above board," said Hazaa Saad, a Shi'ite Moslem from south Lebanon.
In a sign of the times, an African workman is hastily changing the lettering in the name of his shop -- a large warehouse stacked with electronic goods, clothes and crockery.

SOZADIS (the Societe Zairoise de Distribution) has suddenly become SOCODIS (the Societe Congolaise de Distribution), in line with Kabila's decision to change the name of the country to the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Saad and his cousin, Mohamed Hamoud, smile wrily at the homage they are paying to political change.
TRADE GOING WELL
"The important thing is that things have improved. Trade is going very well. Whenever there's a change from a dictator, it's bound to have a good effect on the people," said Saad.

Youssef Mustapha el-Ali, a Lebanese Shi'ite shopkeeper from the village of Hariss, said the advent of Kabila, besides bringing down the dollar, really had simplified dealings with the local administration.

"In Mobutu's day, when you had a fee to pay, you went to some office in a back street and the money disappeared into somebody's pocket. Sometimes it was impossible to meet all the demands people made," he said. "Now you just go to the bank and do it properly," he added.

Ali, whose small shop sells clothes, second-hand shoes, cassette tapes, cosmetics and other odds and ends, does have one chore to satisfy the new authorities. He is photocopying his passport to renew his residence permit, even though the old regime gave him one valid till 1999.

The Lebanese said none of those in Lubumbashi were thinking of leaving. "Personally I hope to stay a long time. It's a good country, very rich. It could be the richest in Africa," said Lebanese Naji Fayad, who gave up a life in Canada four years ago to join his relatives in Africa.
"I'm not going home now," said Hagigeorgiou. "There's too much business. Anyway, when I go to Cyprus, I find all my friends have gone. Now I have all my friends here."
